messages.subject: one vs. multiple chain diagnostics
parts:
This originally came from an issue discussion. We're trying to
keep our issues focused on actionable issues, not general discussion,
so I'm moving this here.

The only reason to run a single chain that I can imagine is when
there's persistent multimodality and you're happy with a single mode and
can't easily merge multiple chains because of things like index switching and
you want to do inference dependent on the mixtures, as in creating one
of those word clouds from an LDA model or something like that.

I believe Ben's the one who wrote the pairs() plot in RStan and I'm not
sure what his intent was. Maybe he can clarify.

- Bob

> On Apr 18, 2016, at 5:11 PM, Chris Black <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> I hope this isn't getting too far afield, but in that case I'm curious what the best practice is for diagnostics. My current application is a model with persistent divergence warnings and periodically stuck chains, which I thought I had gathered was a case where I'd want to run a single chain, examine par-vs-accept, and fix the model to make one chain look good before I worry about convergence/parallelism. Is that not the case, or are you just saying single chains call for different plotting methods?

I should have said I do want multiple chains from the final model; I’m just wondering if it can help debugging. In a case where initialization looks OK but the sampler is having trouble exploring the whole posterior with any one chain, does adding more chains make it easier or harder to isolate the problematic part of the model?

>

Sorry, I think I’m missing the connection here. The issues in my original report were with stan_diag() and stan_par() — as far as I can tell pairs() works nicely with any number of chains, including 1.

Thanks,

No problem at all. We'd much rather get feedback than no feedback,
even if we want to move channels.

>> The only reason to run a single chain that I can imagine is when
>> there's persistent multimodality and you're happy with a single mode and
>> can't easily merge multiple chains because of things like index switching and
>> you want to do inference dependent on the mixtures, as in creating one
>> of those word clouds from an LDA model or something like that.
>
> I should have said I do want multiple chains from the final model; I’m just wondering if it can help debugging. In a case where initialization looks OK but the sampler is having trouble exploring the whole posterior with any one chain, does adding more chains make it easier or harder to isolate the problematic part of the model?

Yes, multiple chains can help you find multiple spots in the posterior that
may be problematic. And problems won't show up on every chain in every model.
They'll also show when you're not converging, which can be hard to diagnose
with a single chain that's not moving well.

I've found the pairs() plots to be most useful, because you can see strong
dependencies and nasty banana shaped marginal posteriors for pairs of paramters.

>> I believe Ben's the one who wrote the pairs() plot in RStan and I'm not
>> sure what his intent was. Maybe he can clarify.
>
> Sorry, I think I’m missing the connection here. The issues in my original report were with stan_diag() and stan_par() — as far as I can tell pairs() works nicely with any number of chains, including 1.

You're right --- pairs() works with one chain now. I believe it used
to require more than one by default.

- Bob
